1763762: During boarding Flight Attendant B let me know there was a passenger who was speaking on her cell phone while not wearing a mask. Flight Attendant B asked her to put the mask on and the passenger said she can't talk on the phone through a mask. Flight Attendant B insisted and the woman begrudgingly put the mask on. As I passed by the passenger she was again not wearing the mask and speaking on her phone. I stood by the seat in front of her waiting for a good break in the conversation for a time to talk with her and she wrapped up the conversation and said sorry and put the phone away. I told her it wasn't an issue with the phone, but the health and safety of those around her. She put her mask on. Shortly thereafter as we were preparing the cabin for departure I noticed her mask was below her nose. She was wearing her headphones and did not hear me, but when she saw me she pulled the mask up over her nose. Based on the attitude she gave Flight Attendant B and the fact that the mask was off again when I came by, and then not properly worn a third time Flight Attendant B and I concurred that if we had to speak with her again it would merit a disciplinary action. We also told the flight deck this, so that they would be aware. Throughout the flight we did have close eyes on her, as one does when a passenger has already exhibited behavior that is against the rules, but I tried not to hound on her. During service I saw her and some others wearing their mask below their nose or off in the long times between sips and I made a PA asking everyone to be compliant (in no way singling her out).Once it came time for final compliance for landing I came back through and again her mask was fully below her nose. I stopped and kneeled down and told her that we had already spoken with her about the mask and that wearing it under the nose does not comply. During the conversation that followed she did not pull her mask over her nose until after I had walked away.She told me that she has a medical condition that makes her light headed and that she has been doing her best with the mask. I told her that while for several months we had mask exemptions for medical cases for the last month it has been mandatory regardless of individual. She asked me for my full name and asked if she could take a picture of my name tag. I told her I was not comfortable giving my last name but if she reached out to the company they would know who I was. She said that I was rude for hounding her and briefly said the word 'Nazi' in reference to my strict adherence to the mask policy and 'targeting' of her.The specifics of timing between what was said during this conversation and what was said in the conversation after I brought disciplinary action and later during final compliance all kind of meld, but these things were said.She said that it was wrong to single out people who have medical conditions and that they don't have to share what the condition is. I reminded her that at no point did I ask her what her condition is and that she only shared that she had a condition at the end of the flight after things came to a head. I also explained again that regardless of condition the mask policy is for anyone who wants to fly.Some guests in the nearby rows thanked me for sticking to the policy as they had had concerns with the passenger in question not wearing her mask throughout the flight. I did my best to thank them for their support, but also to not rile up the non-compliant passenger nor the woman across the aisle who seemed to have befriended and come to the passenger's side (however this woman never spoke up to me or in my earshot). I did not want to put passengers against each other or cause more disruption.Passenger also said that she was not planning on flying [Airline] ever again. We let the Captain know [of the situation] and he called ahead to have a Supervisor meet passenger. During deplaning several of the other passengers that were in surrounding seats and had spoken up again thanked me for the way I handled the situation and said they'd be writing in to the company. Passenger was sitting in seat XX1. When securing the cabin before door closure she was on phone and had mask looped on one ear and hanging down and I asked her to put it on she said 'but I can't talk on the phone with it' and I said 'I apologize but it has to be worn over your nose and mouth at all times it is our policy' then she just looked at me with an attitude and then I asked her again if she could please put it on to which she said 'sssuurrreeee' and put it on. Then I informed another FA and told him to keep an eye on her and then he immediately walked through the cabin and she had it off again, not even one minute later. So he also asked her to put it on. After safety demo passenger had mask on but not covering her nose FA A asked her to pull it up and make sure it is covering both her nose and mouth.Inflight there were times she took exaggerated time to eat and drink. As were others in the cabin so we made a PA, (overall I bet we made 20 mask policy PAs during the entire flight).Then during descent FA A observed her with it off again. I seen him having a conversation with her so I approached and he mentioned to her the policy and the reasons and the procedure and then told her he would be back.He said she said she knows the policy. And around that time she mentioned to him that she was trying her best but she has a medical condition. She continued to argue with him and ask for his name to file a complaint. Passengers in front of and behind her gave thanks to FA A for enforcing the policy and said he handled it well. I do believe she overheard them praising him. We notified Captain and he informed [the] arrival station.

1763777: Aircraft X had a tail pipe fire on Number 2 engine. [Maintenance] troubleshot the issue and found the oil over serviced. The aircraft did an RON (Remain Overnight) in ZZZ. The engines were oil serviced twice. Suggest [safety reports] from both techs on the log pages attached.
1763787: VFR departure normal. Right turn at shoreline. I departed with flight following but was informed ATC would be too busy along my route and was told to squawk VFR. Limited to the Class Bravo shelf, I set my altitude select to 4500 ft. and engaged the autopilot in the climb. Monitoring the climb, I saw the plane continue the climb past 4500 ft. and where I expected it to settle back to 4500 ft., instead go through 4600 ft. upon which I disengaged the auto pilot and pushed on the yoke. However, the trim up elevator wouldn't relax, I couldn't turn the trim wheel and all I could do was push hard against the yoke as I busted Bravo and the plane climbed at least another 400 ft. with the trim stuck. I pulled the circuit breaker but it still wouldn't release and I manually pushed the yoke hard to get the plane below the bravo. I cycled the breaker and the switch and finally got the trim under control. I hand flew at 4500 ft. until passing the shelf and continued on my flight climbing to 8500 ft. with no difficulties. Later, I determined that I have a faulty autopilot altitude switch. Getting it fixed tomorrow. In retrospect, I feel I handled the problem calmly but expeditiously.
1763798: There are way too many airfields in Central/South Florida that are in somewhat close proximity on the same CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency) frequency 123.05. These airfields include GIF Winter Haven, 2IS Airglades, X04 Apopka, PCM Plant City, X26 Sebastian, and X39 Tampa North. On busy days usually towards the end of the week including Thur, Fri, Sat and Sun when the weather is good and many people are out flying, this frequency is completely jammed up much of the day with radio calls from all of the different airfields all at once. It is difficult sometimes to even get a quick call in. Some of these airfields to include GIF, PCM, X04 and X26 are very busy with flight school traffic, local GA (General Aviation) traffic and skydiving (at X26). This creates an unsafe situation when pilots cannot even hardly get a word in on CTAF to give a standard traffic call. Often times pilots will step on each other making calls which creates a jamming type sound which further makes comm more difficult. There shouldn't be this many airfields this close on the same frequency.
1763803: Went out for practice approaches. 1763812: On final approach to Runway 20 at ICL there are grain bins in the flight path with the red obstacle [light] burned out. I have requested for weeks that it be fixed, but has not as of today. 1763817: During a routine IFR training flight and upon departure from 0S9 (Port Townsend, WA - Jefferson County Intl), we were following the published Obstacle Procedure like we have many numerous times in training and filing IFR. On this day, it was Intermittent IMC above 1500 and VFR under and notable that day was 20 knots plus winds aloft from the Northwest. Upon departure from Runway 09, take off and turning right to heading 090 and in the climb, Turbulence and Tailwind were increasing, and IMC Conditions now present in and out of Cloud Banks. When I went to intercept the 166 radial off the Penn Cove VOR turning North, what was now strong tail winds and light to moderate chop, quickly became a pronounced quartering tail wind with well defined moderate turbulence present. I became disoriented with the leans as the plane was not easily coming level. This created the beginning of an unusual attitude that was best corrected by recovering out of the right turn and remaining in said turn to get back on what was now the controllers vectors of 320 vs As Filed, I was able to recover from this and then began working to comply with ATC as they were inquiring why we were deviating course. I explained to the controller after the plane was stable and back on course that I had entered IMC in Turbulence and experienced spatial disorientation and had to recover. Once the plane neared 4,000 MSL, turbulence lightened, and I was able to proceed on course and as filed to Friday Harbor with no further issue. The rest of the day we experienced strong winds into Bellingham and then back into Port Angeles but nothing else of note. I am writing this to call out what I learned and what I also believe is a risk to myself and other pilots. I believe this Obstacle Departure Procedure places aircraft and pilots while under a potentially heavy workload in IMC in an area that is well known and proven for strong weather convergence with little to no information to fully assess conditions in such a micro climate. I believe there is a safety issue here that could be mediated by reducing the greater than 45 degrees requirements that exists today from 090 degrees bearing to intercepting the 166 Radial and a 346 Bearing. This ODP creates risk and added another link in the chain against me that day, with the strong quartering wind, and turbulence created an unusual attitude and deviation to course. The Instructor and I briefed on what went right and wrong there. We concluded that unusual attitude training cannot be emphasized enough as part of initial and continued training. We also agreed that the use of the Autopilot in heading mode would have helped avoid this situation as I was hand flying through the strong quartering and side wind/turbulence. I also called out that the aircraft has a leaning tendency to the right which I believe was not a key item, but could have added another link in the chain as it may have magnified the strong action the plane took to shift/turn to the right. I am having a Mechanic from a certified service center further evaluate to ensure the plane is in proper rigging beyond what was observed in the last annual inspection.

1763842: ZZZ1 started a side-stream handoff on Aircraft X at 60,000 ft. to ZZZ ARTCC. Center flight plan showed the route of flight ZZZ5 […] ZZZ5. The flight plan showed a delay of 4+55 at ZZZ4 and never coming close to ZZZ. The pilot ended up on an incorrect ZZZ UHF frequency and they in turn shipped the aircraft to the correct sector frequency which was the sector that the aircraft was in. The CIC (Controller in Charge) called the ZZZ1 supervisor to try and figure out the route of flight. The CIC was unsuccessful in finding out what the exact route of flight was. I was told about the situation and I directed our TMU (Traffic Management Unit) to contact ZZZ1 TMU to try and determine what the aircraft's intentions were. ZZZ MOS (Military Operation Specialist) was able to contact ZZZ1 MOS and they faxed a depiction of the route of flight which had no flight plan information. The depiction showed the aircraft flying southeast after ZZZ2 but the map did not have the range to display ZZZ's portion of the flight. I called the ZZZ1 Operation manager who was not aware of the situation. The ZZZ1 MOS provided a point of contact (Person A) for the mission. I called Person A and he was unwilling to provide the route of flight. I explained that this aircraft was in controlled airspace and the controllers had no idea where the aircraft was going. By this time the aircraft was 190 miles inside of our airspace. He said that he was unable to provide the route of flight on an unsecured line. He said that the aircraft was going to go a little bit further east and then make a loop back to ZZZ2. Then he said that the aircraft was going to go to ZZZ3 and make a loop. I said that he obviously knew what the points along the flight plan was and that is what I was looking for. He again was unwilling to provide the route of flight. I inquired about this 'loop'. I asked if the aircraft was making a left turn direct ZZZ2 after ZZZ3. We were concerned about the aircraft turning right into Mexico. Person A stated that a loop meant that the aircraft would do one turn in holding with a 30 mile leg at ZZZ3. Then he stated that the pilot may make another loop 100 miles east of ZZZ2 before heading to ZZZ2. Person A stated that this was all coordinated with ZZZ1. I explained that the aircraft is now over 200 miles inside of ZZZ's airspace and that we have no coordination of what is happening. The aircraft flew from ZZZ2 to ZZZ3 where the pilot made a left hand turn in holding and then proceeded to the ZZZZZ area and made a right hand turn in holding and then back into ZZZ1 airspace.ZZZ put in a route that would get the datablock to process back to ZZZ1 but was still not the exact routing that the pilot was cleared. We never did figure out what the route of flight was. ZZZ1 needs to properly update an aircraft's route of flight before making a handoff. These types of missions need to be coordinated with ZZZ's airspace and procedures office before the mission begins.
1763863: I received a call from the Purser that they had an e-cig (e-cigarette) overheat/explode in seat pocket. He said a non-rev Captain who was seated in area removed the passengers from row and sprayed the seat pocket with a halon fire extinguisher. He said he heard a loud pop and saw a flash. He immediately cleared the passengers and sprayed the seat pocket area with a Halon that a flight attendant handed him. 1763875: During vectors to ICN we got a delay due to unauthorized drone activity. Approach Control was unable to predict the length of the delay. We immediately began evaluating options for fuel and landing. After being vectored for around 10-15 minutes Captain made the decision to declare minimum fuel. Landing was uneventful. Apparently there was drone activity near RKSI which prevented aircraft from landing. Without any clear time frame as to when we would be landing and being number 7 for landing we made the decision to divert. Don't really have any. Can't control rogue drone activity.
1763881: During the walk around, my First Officer discovered oil leaking from multiple points inside the number one engine exhaust area. 1763885: I was conducting a visual approach to [Runway] XXR backed up by the RNAV Y XXR. I was the Pilot Flying and the Captain was the Pilot Monitoring. We had briefed all the threats and the approach per the AOM prior to the TOD and were planning flaps full for the landing configuration. We were being vectored onto a base leg to join the final visually. I was faster than I should have been on the base for the distance we were out (180 selected speed I think) and so I had to delay calling for the flaps. I think the last altitude we were given was 8,000 feet on the base before we reported the field in sight and were cleared for the visual. The approach had been activated and I went to managed speed. We then set a lower altitude just above the altitude for the next fix after the one just ahead of us on the approach so I could use vertical speed to start down and stay on the path since the approach was not quite captured. I had armed the approach and it annunciated FINAL APP as we were joining the final and the aircraft continued descending on the path. I was using the auto pilot for lateral and vertical NAV until established on final. We extended the gear prior to joining the final to help with slowing the aircraft to flap deployment speeds. The vector had put us in closer than I had anticipated and I had also started slowing later than I should have. The speed did not come back very quickly, possibly because of a tailwind shifting to a headwind as were turning final, so I had to disconnect the autopilot and arrest the descent to get the aircraft slowed for flap deployment and also to prevent an overspeed. Both the Captain and I noticed the RA was close to 1,000 [feet] as we deployed final flaps, and our speed was still well above approach speed, but we were VMC and our assessment was that we had been in final configuration prior to 1,000 AGL. We continued the approach and were stable at 500 [feet] so we landed out of the approach within the required criteria. We were at the gate when the ACARS printed a Self-Assessment Flight Report. We weren't surprised to see Y for speed and descent, but we were surprised to see a Y for flap change. We discussed it, and although we were unstable at 1,000 [feet], we felt that we had been configured and thought the report generated a flap change Y at 0974 RA because the terrain rises to the north and the spot elevations are around 300-600 feet higher than the airport elevation near where we selected final configuration. Regardless, the final configuration selection was closer to 1,000 AGL than it should have been and we decided we would file an report just in case. Normally, I call for gear down and managed speed at 2,000 AGL so as to have plenty of time to reach final configuration prior to 1,000 AGL, but I missed that cue because I was in the yellow due to being tighter and faster than I had anticipated, and I didn't realize it because I was busy trying to get back in the green slowing and turning final and descending to stay on the path. This is also a case where my experience exceeded my performance due to being new to being back in the right seat and not flying much in September. I also didn't say anything about being in the yellow, and so I didn't get as much help as I could have used. I also failed to brief that we may need to be configured on base depending on where the base leg is and to say something if I don't ask for the gear down by 2,000 AGL. The other factor was conducting a visual approach to a high-altitude airport where AGL altitudes happen at much higher MSL altitudes than were are used to and neither I nor the Captain had been into ZZZ in a long time. I will more thoroughly brief visual approaches regarding the gates I want for configuration and speed changes that provide plenty of margin for a stabilized approach. As we turned to intercept final and configure for landing with a near 0 VSI, a hill on final gave us an unexpected 1,000 ft. radio alt call. We where visual and comfortable with continuing the approach due to distance. I recall being fully configuration when the second 1,000 foot reading on final and on speed at 500 ft. We failed to slow down in time on base leg not taking into effect high alt difference and ground speed. We did not brief the ground speed difference and the delayed slow down or terrain around the base turn. Haven't been to ZZZ in years.
1763892: During cruise flight, approximately one hour and 30 minutes from landing, a call was received from the cabin regarding a passenger, who was not complying with the face covering policy and disturbing nearby passengers. I asked the A Flight Attendant if any assistance or a diversion will be required, the reply was that more information was needed. A short time later, I received a call from the cabin informing me that the situation had been diffused and that passenger was now compliant.While on approach to landing in ZZZ, I received a call from the cabin stating that passenger was out of his seat creating a disturbance. The A Flight Attendant requested personnel meet the aircraft at the gate. 1763914: The FA (Flight Attendant) came up about 30 minutes prior to departure and said there was a smell, similar to when a gas stove is turned on but not lit, around the exit row. I was eating and asked the FO (First Officer) to go check it out. He came back and said the report was accurate, so I called Maintenance. I was busy eating and asked MX (Maintenance) if he wanted me to write it up, and he said no. He came on and said he had smelled something outside approaching the plane. Once I was done eating, I went back and smelled for myself. It was just as described. The confusing thing was that I had never smelled anything like it before, nor could myself, any passengers, Maintenance or the flight attendants determine what it could be. We continued trying to solve the problem, going up and down the cabin seeing if it was stronger one place versus the other, and seeing if it was dissipating. We did have a family of four leave the flight, English was not their first language so I am unsure if they understood my briefings. As we were dealing with that, we called OPS to notify them of the delay. Shortly after, our mechanic came up and said they noticed a ramp sweeping machine that runs on propane nearby. Then Operations called and said it was a tug nearby that was leaking fuel. With this information, we decided we would pushback and see if it goes away after we left the gate area. We did and checked with the flight attendant twice during taxi to get an update. The first time she said it was dissipating, and on the before takeoff check to the line, she said it was gone. During descent, in the mid-teens, we got a call saying the smell was back. It wasn't busy so we asked for a quicker route to the airport, which was granted and we landed uneventfully. I have no good answer as to why I didn't write this up. I have thought about it since I got off the phone with Maintenance in ZZZ1, and I cannot think of a reason why I decided to not write this up. Referring to [the] manual. Mechanical Irregularities, D. Reporting Mechanical Irregularities, it does not specifically state to write anything in the MX Log. It simply states if the item is notice prior to block out, to contact Maintenance and they will determine the action required to correct or defer the irregularity. I will re-write to read that any time Maintenance is contacted, a write muse ensue. As we were doing preflight duties a FA (Flight Attendant) reported an odd smell in the cabin while passengers were boarding around the exit row. The Captain (CA) asked me to go back and see what I smelled and I did. It was like a natural gas smell mixed with garbage. Nothing I could place a finger on. I reported it to the CA and he went back to check it out. I continued preflight work and he called Mx (Maintenance) out. I didn't hear his and Mx conversation as I continued preflight activities But at the end he told me that the Mx guy could smell it outside and that there was a fuel spill reported from a ground truck in the gate next to us that was the most likely cause of the smell. I continued preflight activities as the Captain finished working with Mx. and he said we were good to depart as long as the smell disappeared when we taxied out. We called the FA on taxi and she said it had dissipated and we departed. On arrival the smell returned and after we reached the gate and shutdown the Captain determined that he had not written up the issue properly in the origin airport before we departed. I believe the Captain was distracted with many tasks and worrying about departing on time which caused him to forget to write up the issue. It's difficult to find a single reason on how to avoid this event. Perhaps more training on specific events that require Mx write ups.

1763953: I was sitting standby and had a mask on for at least 4 hours. It has been a long time since I walked into in-flight. 1763964: While procuring a nitrogen cart to perform aircraft servicing I noticed that the nitrogen bottles loaded into the cart were painted green whereas they are usually an off white color. I immediately suspected that the cart was loaded with oxygen bottles and had to do a quick search to determine that the bottles were in fact nitrogen but they were painted green. The bottles were labeled with a small nitrogen sticker that was on the underside of the bottle. Please see the attached picture. This is a very dangerous condition that would lead to extreme aircraft damage and or human injury/death. A technician could accidentally mistake the nitrogen cart for oxygen and service and oxygen system with nitrogen. Also, a technician could become used to green nitrogen bottles and accidentally service a tire or strut with oxygen. I recommend that these bottles either be taken out of service and repainted, or wrapped with a 360 degree label stating its contents.
1763978: I have flown into MYF several times on an Instrument Approach, ILS 28R. Every time, I am given headings and vectors to final. I have asked for the full approach sometimes, but usually given vectors. The issue is that the altitudes and heading make it very difficult to fly a controlled and standard approach. This last approach I was given a heading to the final approach course at a higher altitude, then turned right and left and then back to final and then a steep descent to be able to get back on the right altitudes for the approach. This has happened about 5 times and usually the same sequence. I am kept high, then a step descent, various headings and then cleared for the approach at the last few minutes. It makes it very difficult to manage speed and altitude. Also, when in instrument conditions it provides an opportunity to become spatially disoriented with the turns and the assigned descent profile. I believe it would be MUCH safer to be given the full approach and follow the listed altitudes. I can tell there is a lot of traffic and a lot of training going on in the area, 2 parallel runways at MYF also present a challenge for controllers, but we should find a way to make the instrument approach be according to the plate. I believe this will make it safer for us all. I respect the Approach controllers and they are dealing with all the traffic the best they can. 1764198: Pilot and a singe passenger were returning for a landing in VMC (winds light and variable), and cleared For landing by Tower. After what appeared to be a normal landing, on-centerline and during roll-out;(the plane was rolling below 30 kts), the aircraft unexpectedly began to pull to the right. The pilot attempted to correct using left rudder pressure and toe brake. The combination of left rudder pressure and left toe brake did not appear to exert sufficient braking authority or correct the turn. The aircraft seemed very slow to correct direction. The pilot continued with left rudder pressure and applied the handbrake. The plane immediately slowed, but rolled off the right side of the marked runway (and onto the apron) as the pilot was able to regain directional control. This was just past the first taxiway, where the underside of the right wing scraped the top edge of the taxiway sign. There did not appear to be any damage to the sign, but the bottom skin of the right wing was later found to be torn, in a line perpendicular to the leading edge, on the outboard side of the wing, about half-way to the from the front of the wing, and the skin tear exposed the bottom edge of the wing spar, which appeared to be nicked. Using the handbrake only from that point on, the pilot was able to return to the runway centerline and taxi the plane on the runway to the next taxiway and then navigate to parking with no further directional control problems. The incident was promptly reported and the plane was grounded for inspection and repair at visual inspection by a qualified A&P.It had been noted that on one prior flight that the plane had unexpectedly pulled to the right, but that the problem had been evaluated and resolved. On pre-flight taxi and takeoff during the flight on which the incident occurred, the plane did not appear to be pulling excessively to the right, so the pilot believed that the earlier squawk had been resolved, and the pilot decided to conduct the flight as planned. The pilot was well-rested, in good health, and alert during the flight. A potential distractor was that the oil access door on the cowling popped open on climb-out after takeoff (this resulted in the decision to return to land and correct the issue before continuing the flight). It is possible that this issue may have distracted the pilot. 1764374: A friend who has a multi engine and instrument rating was interested in possibly buying my Cessna 310 so we flew to breakfast in IMC with me in the left seat acting as PIC. I said we needed to keep coming down, we were nowhere near the altitude we needed to be at to begin the flare, but he leveled off, seeming to feel for the runway from that point. We quickly reached the midpoint of the runway and I began thinking that a go around would be necessary but I let him continue a bit further. Shortly thereafter I called for a go around but he cut the power, raised the nose, and landed firmly, about 2/3 of the way down the runway. I did not think we had room to stop on the remaining runway and at 80 knots we were close to flying speed. He told me to take over and I applied full power. At the end of the runway we still were slower than I would want to be but I raised the nose and we were airborne in ground effect. The plane was very slow to accelerate or climb and I felt my friend pulling back on the yoke. I pushed forward not wanting to stall or leave ground effect. At this point I realized that our gear was still down and that we had landing flaps. I knew that if I retracted landing flaps we had a very strong potential to sink into the ground so faced with that option I left the flaps down. I was not sure of the drag effect from gear retraction so I left it down as well. Again I felt him pulling back on the wheel while I yelled 'stop pulling' and pushed forward.Soon there was a row of trees in the windshield and I gathered we had gotten all of the speed we could for the time being and I pulled back on the yoke. The tower controller had seen what was going on and asked us if we were ok, did we need assistance, and did we see the trees. He also asked if we would be avoiding the trees. These calls were a distraction and I did not answer as my first priority was to fly the aircraft.We climbed out, retracting the gear and flaps. The controller asked if we wanted him to cancel IFR (Instrument Flight Rules) and for us to resume our pattern work. Shaken, I was not interested in pattern work and I asked him to cancel IFR and we would leave the area. Since he had questioned if we had hit the trees I decided to fly about 5 miles to an airport where I have maintenance done to have the plane inspected. Apparently we had made contact with the very top of the tree line as evidenced by some leaves on the nose gear. The mechanic came out to inspect the plane and could find no damage at all after inspecting the gear, flaps, wings, fuselage, and general condition.In retrospect, I had put my friend in a bad position. Even though he had watched me land many times, and had landed himself in the past, I should have demonstrated the first landing. I know better than to land outside the touchdown zone and yet we did. At the midpoint of the runway with limited runway ahead of us, I should have had an aggressive transfer of control and taken the plane around myself. If I had done that I have no doubt I would have raised the gear and flaps allowing a successful climb out, but in the uncertain transfer of control with the pilot monitoring suddenly and unexpectedly becoming the pilot flying, the sequence of a successful go around were lost.I can't help but think that I put the pilot flying into a bad position by not doing the go around sooner and not having the plane in proper climb configuration was a bad error. I have replayed this many times and reminded myself that in this situation, even though you are not the flying pilot, you have to stay on top of things mentally and be prepared to take over at any point.The better decision after the touch down would have been to get out of the mental go around mind set and just kept it on the ground. A couple of blown tires and a plane in the overrun would have been nothing compared to the threats of staggering into the air in a bad configuration with trees ahead.

I felt we had very little angle of attack available - perhaps just enough to climb 10' to clear the fence. I increased elevator as much as I dared, then lowered the nose again once past the fence. Because of our low airspeed and high angle of attack, though the propeller cleared the fence, the top of a fence post contacted and tore the skin of the airplane's belly just aft of the gear legs. As airspeed slowly recovered, I climbed to perhaps 20 feet AGL, then reduced power as we reached the runway and made a normal landing. I have been flying for more than XX years and I have never experienced such a dramatic loss of airspeed. My corrective action to prevent a similar crisis will include the following.1. I will not use the actual beginning of runways to practice power-off landings, but instead have clients treat the touch down zone (1,000 feet down the runway) as their landing target.2. I will be more prepared to push, move, or overpower client pilots if they do not immediately respond to verbal instructions. 3. I will be more mindful of the potential for wind shear, especially when operating downwind of significant obstacles (the wood lot, in this case) on windy days.

Section XX of the bulletin states: VNAV not complying with altitude constraint during approach. When the last waypoint of a STAR procedure is common to the first waypoint of the instrument approach procedure, the FMS may automatically meld the waypoints. The altitude constraints contained in both procedures for that particular waypoint is expected to be melded as well. In other scenarios, the last STAR waypoint contains a 'fly vectors to intercept' leg. This waypoint can also be the first one for the approach procedure and the pilot may manually delete the 'fly vectors' or copy the approach waypoint of the same waypoint on the STAR, which will also meld both waypoints.Embraer has received reports of the airplane not complying with the published altitude constraints during transition from STAR to instrument approach procedure. Investigations have revealed that an altitude violation may occur when two common waypoints are melded, either automatically by the FMS or manually by the pilot, where the last waypoint of the STAR and the first waypoint of the approach procedure has the same name, but different altitude constraints. As a consequence, the FMS constructed vertical flight path may not respect the altitude constraint, despite the altitude constraint indications of the FMS FLT PLAN page, VSD (Vertical Situation Display) and PFD (Primary Flight Display) are correctly displayed. The VNAV guidance may result in a constructed flight path above or below the published constraint. To prevent the violation of an altitude constraint, after a common waypoint is melded automatically by the FMS or manually by the pilot, perform as follows, Delete the altitude constraint at the melded waypoint, manually re-insert the altitude constraint in the FMS.

1764964: During a flight to maintain currency an upset event occurred. Aircraft X took off from ZZZ on a VFR flight with flight following. ATC apologized for the delay and cleared Aircraft X to proceed on course. Leveling off at 5,500 feet MSL and after visually and electronically checking for traffic, setup for slow flight and approach to stall practice. Retarded throttle, airspeed was already below 165 knots so landing gear was extended, verified all gear was down and locked. Held altitude while speed bleed off, applying flaps incrementally until fully extended. Began stabilized slow flight, adjusting throttle and pitch as necessary to maintain 5,500 feet. Winds at 5,500 MSL were 18 knots and there was some light turbulence. After 1-2 minutes of steady slow flight the airspeed indicator dropped quickly even though there were no rapid throttle or control surface adjustments. The stall horn began sounding continuously and the aircraft experienced very slight buffeting at which point full throttle and downward pitch were applied simultaneously and in the same instant the right wing dropped extremely rapidly as if the aircraft had been commanded into a snap roll. The roll continued even as left aileron and left rudder were applied with no effect and in less than 2 seconds the aircraft was inverted. At this point the nose dropped and the aircraft entered a right-hand spiral dive. The throttle was immediately retarded and standard recovery efforts begun. Attempts to level the wings were complicated by the g-forces as the pilot struggle to remain upright. At least 5-7 right hand turns occurred in spite of left aileron input. At approximately 500-700 feet AGL, control was reestablished and the aircraft returned to zero roll. A climb was initiated and as the airspeed dropped the pilot remembered the aircraft was still in full landing configuration with the throttle at idle. Power was added, flaps retracted one notch and the landing gear was retracted. Continued retracting flaps one notch at a time as speed and altitude increased.After returning to a safer altitude, all aircraft controls were checked and seemed to be normal with no apparent explanation for the un-commanded roll. Only after landing and examining the aircraft was the extreme damage noted. Apparently during the spiral dive, the aircraft exceeded speed and g-force limitations even though the pilot does not recall an overspeed warning.
1764966: I had flown several days prior to ZZZ2 past Yakima and passed West of Boardman (R-5701) making sure to avoid that restricted airspace. I never even realized I was in restricted airspace or I would have turned around. I was climbing throughout the time in the R-6714A area and did not reach my altitude of 6,500 feet until I was pretty much out of it as near as I can recall. We were also busy watching for other airplanes in the haze recognizing that some still do not have ADS-B. We did not encounter any aircraft in the [area].We flew home without incident and landed at ZZZ shortly after XB00. One aircraft was in front of us upon landing. Since neither I nor my wife had heard anything I did not know what to think. Later I was wondering if they had but couldn't understand why they would have had reason. I decided to return to my hanger and get my tablet out to review my flight. At that time I realized that I had unknowingly flown directly through R-6714A, a huge no- no. That is when I called ZZZ Ops and they passed me onto Approach who passed me to Center. I spoke with a staff member and made sure he had all the information needed. He assured me he had what he needed to finish his part and the case would then move to FSDO.Having realized what a blunder I had made I began to reconstruct all my actions and thinking that got me into flying into R-6714A without realizing I was in restricted airspace. I would never have know had Seattle Center and ZZZ1 not followed me home to ZZZ1. Of course, I fully realize there are no secrets as I have ADS-B. I know the whole things falls onto me for not having paid more attention to the map. Lesson learned is that I need to pay more attention. I think I got complacent in thinking I knew the area because I had flown by ZZZ3 many times through the years, but not by this airspace. I use FlyQ EFB and keep on top of being current so that system provides the correct data for me to note, I just need to pay more attention to it. I will explore if it can be more helpful by informing me when I am about to fly into airspace that is controlled. I also think as pilots we pay more attention now to the ADS-B Traffic we get on our tablets than to what the map is sharing below that traffic. I wonder if we shouldn't be having more training on tablets and their use in the cockpit. In summary, I regret that my incursion interfered with a military exercise and hope that the distraction was minimal. I am not fond of these kinds of hard lessons and will work to make sure that does not happen again. I also apologize for the extra work everyone is doing as a result of this incursion. I hope my story can be useful in improving safety.

The PF directed me to extend the gear to assist with the descent and speed. Just prior to EEDGR we received a SINK RATE alert, and the PF shallowed the descent slightly, so we crossed EEDGR at approximately 200 kts and 3,600 ft. At the appropriate speeds, I extended the flaps, and shortly above 1,000 ft. AGL (Above Ground Level) we received a TERRAIN PULL UP alert, at which point I called for a go-around, which the PF executed. We climbed to 3,000 ft, ran the appropriate checklists, and then made a normal visual approach and landing.As we crossed EEDGR, the PF dialed the AAD to TDZE (Touch Down Zone), allowing the aircraft to continue descending while we attempted to get on profile.The PF and I were both distracted attempting to configure the aircraft and meet the profile of the approach. We both felt that the altitude and airspeed assignment at YOLOW made the switch to the REQUIRED visual approach with RNAV waypoints very difficult, and if we had simply flown a normal visual approach (which we've been doing for 15 years), we would have been fine. In the future, I will refuse a clearance to cross YOLOW at 7,600 ft and 250 kts if I expect to fly the visual to Runway 21. I feel the [Company] procedure as published actually reduces safety by drawing one or both pilots' attention into the cockpit during a critical phase of flight.

1765081: ZZZ Arrival ATIS C was current, advertising visual approaches to Runways XYL, XXL, and XXR. Prior to descent the Captain and I had thoroughly briefed visual approaches to both Runway XYL and Runway XXL. We requested Runway XXL on initial contact with ZZZ TRACON and were granted the request before ZZZZZ on the ZZZZZ2 STAR. We were vectored after ZZZZZ1 onto a left base to Runway XXL, then a turn to join final, which accompanied the visual approach clearance and change to Tower on [frequency]. I called Tower advising we were on a visual approach to Runway XXL and would be parking at gate. Tower responded with 'Runway XXL, cleared to land.' About a minute later, I noted that Tower instructed traffic to cross Runway XXL downfield at either Taxiway V or Taxiway R without referencing us, which I noted as strange. While on final, I noticed that a different aircraft had pulled up to the hold short line for Runway XXL at Taxiway Y10, and that I had not yet heard that crew interact with Tower. When we were on approximately a 1-mile final, the crew of the aircraft holding short called Tower advising they were ready for departure. Without referencing us, Tower stated 'RNAV to ZZZZZ3, Runway XXL, cleared for takeoff.' As soon as we heard this, the Captain stated to me that we would be going around, and we recited the first 3 calls we would make when that happened. I keyed up on the radio and stated 'Traffic on short final, Runway XXL.' By then the departing aircraft had entered the runway. Tower responded with go around instructions including a right turn to a 270 heading and a climb to 4,000. I read them back, and the Captain and I properly executed a go-around. I cleared the right side of the aircraft for any traffic landing XXR, noted there was none, and stated 'Clear on the right.' As we began the turn, TCAS sounded a traffic advisory. I noted the yellow target on TCAS was indicating 800 feet, and stated aloud that the traffic had just lifted off and that we could disregard the advisory, as we were turning away. Tower apologized for the mistake and sent us to approach for re-sequencing and an uneventful visual approach and landing on Runway XXR.The crew of the departing aircraft appears to have failed to visually check the final for traffic before calling Tower for a takeoff clearance, and again prior to taxiing onto the runway for departure. The Air Traffic Controller appears to have forgotten about having cleared us to land, or appears to have been situationally unaware of our position prior to issuing the takeoff clearance. The Runway Status Lights (RWSL) on Runway XXL appear not to have worked, either because my aircraft's position on short final failed to trigger the red stop bars, because the departing aircraft ignored the RWSL red stop bars, the RWSL malfunctioned, or because the system was improperly overridden by the Controller. Another system that appears to have failed is the Controller's ASDE-X safety logic, because it appears my radio transmission was the primary reason he initiated the go-around instructions. Typically, when departing traffic crosses the hold short line with an arriving aircraft on short final, ASDE-X safety logic sounds an alarm. An additional contributing factor is the resurgence of traffic levels after a significant prolonged drop stemming from the outbreak of COVID-19, which may have led to complacency on the part of the departing crew and the Controller.Departing crews need to diligently check the final for traffic before taxiing onto the runway for takeoff, and ideally before even calling ready for departure. Failing to do so before calling ready violates basic airmanship and sets the Controller up for failure. That said, the Controller should have had use of a memory aid or reliable automation to indicate and help him remember that Runway XXL was being used as an active arrival runway, that we had been issued a clearance to land, and that we were on short final to that runway at the time heissued the departing aircraft's takeoff clearance. Interviewing the crew of the departing aircraft would also shed light on whether the RWSL had illuminated and, if so, whether they proceeded onto the runway with the RWSL stop bars illuminated. If this is the case, retraining would mitigate this event from happening again. Interviewing the Controller would provide insight as to whether he overrode the RWSL, whether the ASDE-X safety logic worked properly, and other details about the work conditions that shift including staffing and fatigue, which, if undesirable, could be corrected to help mitigate the recurrence of this event.

1765176: We started our takeoff roll at ZZZ. It was the FO's (First Officer's) leg. Shortly after the 'set takeoff thrust call' my window on the Captain's side started to slide open. I'd estimate our speed at 40 kts. It was barely open so I said 'continue' and reached up to close it. However, the window would not close and actually felt like it was coming out of the track. I assumed the window would easily close and that we still had plenty of time to safely reject at low speed if it wouldn't. At that point I became distracted and was worried that the window was falling in. At that point the FO asked if I wanted to reject and I said 'yes'. He initiated the reject as he saw that I was handling the window. As I brought my scan away from the window the reject was started and I noticed the airspeed was about 100 kts. The aircraft quickly decelerated as it was very light. I expected the airspeed to be less than 80 kts based on the short amount of time we had been rolling. The FO continued to stop the aircraft. At that point I took controls. He called the Tower and I made a PA to the passengers to remain seated. We then taxied off the runway at Taxiway X and coordinated with Maintenance to have the brakes checked. They gave us a thumbs up and we taxied to the gate. At that point the window was stuck in a half open position. We shutdown at the gate and switched to another aircraft. Rejecting immediately when the window started to slide open would have prevented the distraction and the rejection would have started at a slower speed. I assumed two things: that the window would easily close and that we were still below 80 kts when the decision was made. It may have been, but at the light weight the aircraft accelerated quickly and I think by the time the actions began we were over 80 kts. At approximately 40 kts during takeoff roll, Captain side window slid open. Captain called continue and attempted to close the window. A few seconds later I looked over and saw the Captain was struggling to get it closed. I stated that I recommend we reject and he agreed. His hands were still on the window to prevent it from slamming back so I initiated the reject procedure. I did not notice the top airspeed, but I would estimate visually about 100 kts, autobraking did engage. Aircraft came to a stop abeam Taxiway X. Notified the Tower. We were instructed to exit on Taxiway. We stopped on Taxiway and called Company. Maintenance met us on ramp and checked the brakes. We taxied in. Window was unable to be shut. When Maintenance came to the flight deck and were able to move the window forward the handle seemed loose and the squeeze grip seemed loose so we all conferred and removed the aircraft from service.I specifically remember observing the Captain check his window just prior to calling for the before takeoff checklist so I think it was secure. We should have rejected as soon as the window slid open to prevent from getting to the higher speed. The aircraft was light so acceleration was very rapid.

Captain confirmed max speed of 230 knots from QRH, so we slowed to 220 to provide a margin. The slat/flap indicator showed slats were almost up, significantly less than 1. We lowered gear to burn down gas to below max landing weight. While still in holding, we selected flaps 1 and obtained normal indications on the slats. Once all briefings, checklists and QRH procedures were complete, the Captain resumed flying duties and I requested to exit holding and obtain vectors for approach to Runway XX. We did not declare an emergency because the aircraft seems to have a computer or indication problem and slats lowered normally once we started to configure. In retrospect, any flight control problem is reason to declare emergency, but not sure if we then should undeclared once all was normal. I have not flown much in the past 7 months, so I may have reverted to previously learned procedures.Any flight control issue is an emergency, even when corrected. Better maintenance on aircraft.

1765267: On Sunday, (date) I was called off reserve to fly Aircraft X under Ops Spec XXXX, with a ferry permit, from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. 1765273: Normal day, normal passenger operations, on Aircraft X, performing ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight. With APU being under MEL, started engine number one at the gate according to normal checklist. Cleared to push out of the gate, to the blue line. The initial push back was mostly smooth. Aircraft pushed on a slant angle on the green line and stopped. Tow truck driver contacted the flight deck, stating that he will pull us to the blue line. Since then, the mild tensions and sounds were sensible as if it felt that the angle of pulling forward to the blue line was kind of steep. I, personally, could not see the tow truck from the right seat. Shortly after, we heard a bigger noise and aircraft started to move forward that followed immediately by the driver asking us to set the brake in a rushed voice, Captain acted promptly, and we stopped the aircraft on time and smoothly. I personally did not feel any impact. We stopped with an angle on the blue line. The driver mentioned that the tow bar broke and he is going to disconnect and contact the ramp safety. We communicated with the Ramp, Operations and MX (Maintenance) Control. Captain communicated with the flight attendants and made an announcement to the passengers informing them about the nature of problem. Within 10 minutes or so, with the supervision of our MX personnel on the ground, a new tow truck, new tow bar and a new driver towed us back to the same gate. This time it was very smooth. We found out that a scratch line and a shallow dent exist on the lower right-hand side of the aircraft. It happened by the shallow impact of the fuselage with the roof of the tow truck. Captain wrote up the damage in MX logbook. Dispatch and Flight Operations have been informed. Everybody acted professional during and after the event. Don't know if the tow bar breaking happened because of the angle & the tension exposed to it, or it was the material failure. Tail swap happened shortly after, and we performed the same flight on ship (tail). If a tow truck driver is not happy with the location of the aircraft or if for some reason they are in a tight spot, or any other unusual issue, they can always consider us as a team and communicate any unease with us, so we all figure out how to get out of it. My assumption is that if we were unhooked from the tow bar on the green line, the entire event could have been avoided. It could only cost me a simple radio call to the ramp, I guess. These are my recollections as I remember them: We were operating Aircraft X operating out of gate X. Aircraft X was operating with MEL APU Inoperative applied. We complied with procedures for engine start with external pneumatic air source & completed the appropriate normal checklists. Ramp tower assigned us a push back onto the blue line. The push back seemed normal with the exception that the AC (aircraft) was at an odd angle. I attributed this to the push crew having to avoid the construction adjacent to N11. The tug driver announced that he would get us over to the blue line & proceeded to turn the jet that direction. At this point I could sense some stress on the tug/towbar combination but nothing that seemed abnormal. As the driver proceeded towards the blue line the noise the towbar was making got louder until we heard what I'd describe as a pop or snap. At this point the jet rolled forward due to forward momentum & the driver or wing walker said set the brakes. I estimate the jet moved forward about 10 feet as I was applying the brakes. We verified that there were no injuries to any of the push back crew & were informed that everyone on the ramp was safe. I stopped the jet as judicially as I could, taking into account that the FA's (flight attendants) were probably standing, conducting their safety demonstration. The driver announced he needed to have the Ramp Safety Supervisor conduct an inspection & we called Line Maintenance to survey the situation. We called the cabin to verify there were no injuries to guests or crew & subsequently a PA was made by me to inform the guests of our situation. Line Maintenance asked us if we could taxi the jet back to gate under power which I declined, not knowing the extent of any possible damage. A new towbar & tug was connected to the jet & we were towed back to gate. After the checklists were completed I proceeded to do a visual inspection, where I found an approximately 5 foot scrape on the underside of the fuselage, outboard of the right side nose gear door. I made another PA from the L1 door area informing the guests that there would be a tail swap & what our new gate was, then made an AC logbook entry describing the damage I observed. The flight proceeded as normal to ZZZ1 after a 2 hour delay to get everything ready on the jet we swapped into. Not sure if time was a big factor or not. The ramp personnel did not seem rushed but we did push back several minutes after departure time due to the jet being fueled late. Parking an A-321 at [this] gate with the current construction process ongoing may present a challenge to the push back crew due to the longer fuselage & trying to avoid the construction area adjacent to gate. My biggest suggestion would be for the push back crew to communicate any difficulty they may be having with any ground operation. In this circumstance we could have easily stopped the jet, set the parking brakes, & requested a taxi from our current position. We strive to comply with directions given, however, sometimes we need to ask to amend those instructions to meet the current situation.
1765275: Enroute on Aircraft X from ZZZZ to ZZZ we were unable to open the flight deck door. The flight deck crew had requested a bathroom break. The Captain went out and returned normally. However, when the First Officer called to return to the flight deck, the Lead Flight Attendant was unable to open the door. The bottom latch was not unlatching, while the upper latch and mid latch were unlatching normally with the door handle. The flight attendant tried using a metal key to pry the latch open. The Captain tried the unlock switch on the center pedestal. Nothing worked. We communicated with the First Officer and told him the flight deck door was stuck locked. The only option left to us was to pull the pins on the emergency/blowout panel on the door. When this was accomplished the opening allowed the flight attendant to exit the flight deck and the First Officer to return to the flight deck. This was done discreetly but was likely witnessed by some passengers in first class. Once the First Officer was inside the flight deck, the panel was reinstalled and secured with the pins. The rest of the flight continued normally. However, both the Captain and First Officer had to exit the flight deck using the panel once the flight was completed (this was accomplished after all passengers had deplaned) as the flight deck door remain stuck closed and locked. A write up was made in the Maintenance Logbook and the aircraft was turned over to Maintenance. Nothing more to add.The flight crew handled the unusual situation professionally.
1765278: After a successful CAT III landing, we had crossed the two inboard runways and were taxiing north on taxiway towards gate. The FO, who was on the first trip back after one month off, did the after landing flow and confirmed our gate with operations. I thought we were cleared into the gate via spot, but this was not the case.As we were rounding the corner for spot and passing Aircraft Y that was on the line just south of spot, I confirmed with the FO that we were indeed cleared in as I had been distracted switching from low vis taxi diagrams to normal taxi diagrams as the vis was very good, shutting down the Number 2 engine, in addition to the fact that the FO was a soft spoken person. I only mention this as I wasn't surprised I hadn't heard them confirm our clearance to taxi into the gate as I was busy concentrating on the other threats just discussed.As rampers were visible from spot and were marshaling us into the gate, we pulled into the gate normally. Approximately 20 feet short of our final parking spot ground reminded us to contact ramp. We immediately contacted ramp, who was understandably very unhappy with us and we apologized for our error.Needless to say, I take complete responsibility for this incident and am embarrassed I allowed it to happen. I have learned a couple of things from this incident- first, that I need to be extra vigilant when some crew members don't have a lot of recent experience, secondly, when we had discussed that the ground ops were our biggest threat for this CAT III approach, I need to truly take it to heart and be extra cautious to help mitigate the threats present during this segment of our flight.

1765357: Ground Control cleared Flight AB on local IFR flight plan, Flight AB requested own navigation to VOR for full procedure at 2,000 feet. The MVA throughout most of ZZZ airspace is 2,400 feet and normal practice is to clear all IFR aircraft above the MVA. Ground Control did not coordinate the abnormal altitude with Local Control. I did not catch the altitude and due to traffic Flight AB could not get own navigation on departure. I issued a departure heading to Flight AB to avoid traffic that put Flight AB into a MVA of 2,400 feet.Ground Control should only issue IFR aircraft altitudes at or above MVA. Flight AB was assigned 2,000 feet from the Clearance Delivery position on a local IFR flight plan. The request was to fly their own navigation for full VOR Runway XX circle to Runway X approach. Flight AB was assigned a 080 heading on departure that goes into a 2,400 foot MVA area. The weather at the airport was 10 miles/CLR. I climbed the aircraft to 3,000 feet to get them above the MVA and started the process of getting him on course to the VOR for their approach. There was training on Local Control taking place and social distancing guidelines make it difficult for the OJTI to review the strip marking. The 080 heading is near 180 degrees off what the Departure Controller would expect. The Local Controller should coordinate aircraft that are that far out range of their flight plan. Review of strips prior to sending it the approach would help all controllers be on the same page.
1765370: ATC held the flight high. Were given clearance to descend to lower altitude. Aircraft was 7,000 feet high on path. Began expedited descent to catch up to path, ATC then gave level off of FL290. Around FL320, Pilot Flying noticed traffic appear on TCAS below at FL280 and started to adjust vertical descent rate. TCAS RA was triggered for level off. Crew disconnected autopilot and autothrottles and leveled off until traffic was clear, and then continued descent to FL290. Reported RA to ATC. Crew was then notified of aircraft at FL280.ATC was overwhelmed. Perhaps more Controllers are needed in that sector. At the very least, a heads up for aircraft at FL280 would have helped. Crew could have ignored the high on path profile and also descended slower, but that would have caused problems down the road. Switched to a frequency that was very busy. The Controller was overwhelmed, we were getting high on the arrival but couldn't get a word in. Finally cleared to descend, the FO who was Pilot Flying started down with the boards out, but weather ahead didn't allow us to speed up to get down. We were 9,000 feet above profile and coming down when we got a TCAS Alert caused by the descent rate. The FO got busy to alleviate it but by the time he pushed a few buttons, it started saying 'Level Off!' So he disconnected everything and leveled the aircraft off. I told the Controller we were leveling off due to a TCAS conflict, but never got an acknowledgment, because [the Controller] was still constantly talking. After the traffic passed we went to our assigned FL290 and [the Controller] asked '(Call sign) verify your level at FL290.' [Controller] didn't have a clue what just happened. I confirmed we were at FL290 and gave us '...cross ZZZZZ at 9,000 feet…' I said we'd do our best but we'd never make ZZZZZ at 9,000 feet. [The Controller] didn't even acknowledge, so we started hurrying down. When we got switched to Approach frequency I told [the Controller] we'd be high at ZZZZZ and the Controller said 'I know, just do your best and descend to 6,000 feet.'With so many aircraft parked, with so many fewer aircraft flying, why is ATC so min-staffed? It seems the new normal is too few Controllers to handle the traffic that's there.
1765375: Planned landing in BWI on Runway 33L. We were assigned to park at Gate X. On the current ATIS, it had a NOTAM that said 'Taxi F closed between Taxiway P and Taxiway T.' So we had an expectation bias to exit Runway 33L at Taxiway F and that our taxi-in instructions would be to taxi to Gate X via Taxiway P, E, and T. Partly contributing to this expectation was the fact that the last time I flew a month ago, there was also construction on Taxiway T between Taxiways H and F. We also had an additive condition which I briefed at the beginning of the trip that this was my first trip back to work after not flying for 30 days.However, after landing rollout and upon exiting Runway 33L at Taxiway F, we were given instructions by Tower to taxi to Gate X via 'Taxiway P, T to T, and contact Ground.' I thought the Controller had stuttered when he said 'T to T.' So I made the right turn from F to P, thinking he meant 'P, E, T.' We contacted Ground after making the right turn on to Taxiway P. Ground then told us we had turned the wrong way and should have been going the opposite direction on P, then T2, to T. We asked what Taxiway T2 is, since Taxiway T2 is not depicted anywhere on the 10-9 page. He said it is a new taxiway. I do not recall any NOTAMs saying there is a new Taxiway T2, nor where it is located. There was nothing on the ATIS about it.We did not cause any traffic conflicts and held at our current position so that outbound aircraft could taxi out. We were then cleared to our gate without any further incident.In the future, I will remember to stop the aircraft immediately and query ATC whenever there is any doubt or ambiguity in a taxi clearance. Also recommend that the BWI airport advise on their ATIS and their NOTAMs that there is a new Taxiway T2. Furthermore, I would recommend they use a different name for the new Taxiway, as the two different phrases 1) 'T to...' and 2) 'T2' can be easily misconstrued for each other in a verbal clearance.'
1765378: While descending out of 6,000 ft for 4,000 ft, we noticed an aircraft that appeared close to our altitude but slightly lower and appeared to be climbing. I made sure all of our outside lights were illuminated including turning on our landing lights. We then received a TCAS TA alert of proximity and almost at the same time as this received a Traffic Alert 'Climb 6,000 ft and turn 15 degrees right' command from ATC (Approach Control). I then saw the other aircraft turn on his landing light in response to seeing me turn on mine, which told me that he probably saw us too. Shortly thereafter we received a level off command;(RA alert) at which time we did level off. I saw the aircraft passing behind us and returned to the STAR immediately after knowing we would be clear of the conflict. STAR arrival this low and close to such a busy airport should be better protected. Maybe expand the airspace around Austin Airport as it is very busy. I also feel that our air traffic controllers are way over worked and facilities undermanned. ATC does a fantastic job considering but we are expecting too much from these controllers and it will put aircraft and lives at greater risk.
1765382: We were cleared to descend via the arrival except maintain 12,000 ft. We were cruising at 24,000 ft northeast of MOMAR. We began to experience turbulence that resembled wake. At that point in time I was under the impression we were cleared to 12,000 ft. I selected Altitude Intervention to begin a descent out of the turbulence. I selected Altitude Intervention a second time to begin the descent. The crossing attitudes were erased at MOMAR due to selecting ALT Intervene. During both presses of the ALT Intervene the Captain and I VVMI'd. We descended below the published altitude at MOMAR. We briefed the arrival/approach as scheduled and then almost 40 minutes later we began our descent, and inadvertently double pushed and deleted the crossing restrictions at MOMAR. I didn't catch it until we were already out of 24,000 ft.
1765384: Descending via the FLATI 1 RNAV Arrival to Denver, ATC gave us a clearance to cross ELLDO between 17,000 and FL210 (chart restriction is between 16,000 and FL210. We did not know the exact format for that clearance, so the I (PF) (Pilot Flying) programmed in FL180. No wonder we could not remember the format to enter. The B737 Flight Manual states, 'Pilots cannot manually enter or modify altitude restrictions between two altitudes. These types of altitude restrictions are only stored in the navigation database.' This is a problem and causes distraction during a critical and busy phase of flight. This clearance appears to consistently be given, as twice in two days on the FLATI 1 RNAV STAR, the same clearance to cross was given (once landing north, and once south). This time we were landing south. With FL180 in the window, I realize I should have put the bottom available altitude 17,000 feet in. The FMS message came up 'steep descent'. I utilized full speed brake, but went above the path up to 1300 feet. Came down as aggressively as possible and even went slightly faster than the chart speed of 250 knots (did not exceed speed by more than 10 knots). Crossed BSAFE about 200 feet high at around 258 knots.
1765392: The aircraft had preexisting maintenance issues when we received it for dispatch. There was a Class II Flight/Control maintenance message that was defferred. The number 3 IRU was differed from an inbound write up that stated the 'Capt Mach/Airspeed Inop and Nav/Alt discrepancy repeat writeup went to Air Data Capt3 position.' The MEL required that IRU 3 be maintained in the off position. Finally, the First Officer noted a skid mark on the number 1 tire that was subsequently found to be within limits by maintenance. Our Flight was cleared for take off with the Captain flying and Tower indicating that there was a 5 knot tailwind. The 100 knots call out had not yet been made and the thrust levers had been set to FLX/MCT when we received a Level II ECAM. The Captain glanced at the ECAM and noted an Auto Flight Auto Thrust Off ECAM. The Captain elected to continue the take off and to set TOGO thrust. The Captain's thinking at this point was that an Auto Thrust Failure would not affect the ability of the aircraft to fly and that setting TOGO would help with the tailwind. The First Officer then stated that there was another ECAM which indicated an Auto Flight Rudder Travel Limit System Failure. At this point, the V1 call out had not yet been made so the Captain elected to abort the take off. The Captain's thinking at this point was that there was a question now as to the ability of the aircraft to fly since the additional ECAM was potentially a flight control issue and the fact that both ECAMs were received after thrust power had been set. The Captain performed a rejected take off procedure. The aircraft appeared to be under normal control with no other apparent issues so just prior to bringing the airplane to a stop, the Captain instructed the First Officer to make a PA announcement for the passengers to remain seated. The Captain wanted to clear the runway at Taxiway X which is approximately halfway down the 10,187 foot runway but noted to the First Officer that it appeared that the aircraft was not moving forward easily after coming to a stop. At this point the First Officer and Captain discussed the possibility of a tire failure as a potential reason for the difficulty in moving the aircraft but it had not felt like a tire failed. We decided to tell the tower we were going to maintain our position on the runway until we could figure out what the issue was. At this point, we received a call from the flight attendants concerning a faint rubbery/acrid odor that was perceptible in the cabin. The Captain noted that the brake temperatures were still between approximately 450 and 550 degrees Celsius, although increasing, with no other abnormal system indications. The Captain and First Officer discussed that the smell was most likely from the aircraft tires as a result of the rejected takeoff and informed the flight attendants and passengers. The Captain was subsequently able to move the aircraft forward surmising that the aircraft may have been in a low spot on the runway that may have caused the difficulty in moving forward. As the Captain moved the aircraft slowly forward he noted that the aircraft was now moving freely and that there did not appear to be any issues with the tires. The First Officer requested from tower to clear the runway at Taxiway D, we completed our checklists, briefed our passengers and coordinated clearance to hardstand parking Spot 20 so that maintenance could look at the aircraft's condition. Upon arriving at parking Spot 20, the Captain talked with maintenance over the intercom and asked them to inspect the tires and the rest of the aircraft as a result of the rejected take off. Maintenance indicated that there were no visible issues except for the fact that the original skid mark on the number one tire was now larger. After maintenance inspected the aircraft exterior they brought the air-stairs up to door 1L and boarded the aircraft to run maintenance system checks. The wheelswere chocked and the parking brake was released to help cool the brakes. The Captain and Station Manager discussed deplaning the passengers and returning them to the terminal to await the results of the maintenance procedures. The Station Manager did an outstanding job of taking care of our passengers during the deplaning process and also provided our passengers with a complementary meal voucher. The Captain subsequently communicated with Maintenance Control, dispatch and the Duty Manager concerning the rejected take off. The Flight and Cabin crew also debriefed each other concerning the rejected take off. The Captain and First Officer discussed with Maintenance Control what the maintenance plan would be for the aircraft since we were still scheduled to take the aircraft to ZZZ1 and there appeared to be multiple maintenance issues. Maintenance Control indicated that they would perform various checklists and resets. The First Officer advocated that if time permitted that we should attempt to bring in a 320 Systems specialist if possible to answer some of our concerns including why we received the ECAMS after what we thought should have been an inhibited time period after take-off power was set. ALPA Safety reached out to the Captain during this time period so the Captain asked if ALPA Safety could connect the flight crew with an A320 systems specialist to talk about these issues which they did. Maintenance Control subsequently cleared all the maintenance issues with the exceptions of deferring the Auto Thrust system and Class II maintenance messages for Flight/Control and Air Bleed. Maintenance also changed out the number 1 tire due to the skid mark being worse after the rejected take off. We were subsequently dispatched again from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on the same aircraft. Just after take-off roll and beginning the climb out, with the Captain flying, the Captain lost his airspeed and mach indications. The Captain transferred control of the aircraft to the First Officer and the First Officer continued the climb out. The Flight then received a Nav/Alt Discrepancy ECAM. We performed the checklist. In order for us to restore the Captain's Airspeed/Mach indication we had to select Air Data Capt3 for the Captain just like the previous write up. We also had to select the First Officers Auto Pilot 2 since the Captains Auto pilot 1 would level off 500 feet off altitude. We Contacted Dispatch to get a phone patch to Maintenance Control and told Maintenance Control we were still having Air Speed, Mach and altimeter issues for the Captains side and wrote up the issues. We then proceeded to ZZZ1 with no further issues. Rejected takeoff due to multiple ECAMs which were triggered and addressed as we transitioned from low speed to high speed regime. The reject actions were as per SOP and the flight attendants thanked us for a prompt Remain Seated, Remain Seated notification. Taxi back to ramp and a multi-hour maintenance delay ensued.
1765395: Received aircraft from maintenance base in ZZZ with AFT FUEL BOOST PUMP MEL. Called and got another Dispatcher to patch Captain to Maintenance Control. Still did not get my answer about having to carry an extra 5,000 pounds of unusable fuel. Flying with a First Officer who was on different aircraft. Very little recent experience in aircraft, because of the COVID and personnel issues. Slowed pace considerably to accommodate, First Officer [was] very hard on himself and working hard on flows, but not smooth and habit like. Dark on departure, and with amber fuel pump light shining in my eye, I did not catch the switch out of place after the Before Takeoff Checklist was done and we took the runway for takeoff. After takeoff, it seemed very early the airplane went into nav mode, with a right turn. Before I could say anything my Captain was correcting the turn. And before that ATC told us to turn left to 350. He then mentioned we were supposed to turn left on the ZZZX not right. We apologized and continued without incidence. Cause - Second flight on over 7 months, due to COVID. A bunch of cockpit distractions, followed by multiple different clearances, and airplane malfunctions with automatic uploads.
